arXiv:2509.14255v1 [cs.CL] 12 Sep 2025

Opening the Black Box: Interpretable LLMs via Semantic Resonance Architecture

Ivan Ternovtsii Affiliation: Department of Information Technologies Affiliation: Uzhhorod National University, Ukraine Affiliation: HengeBytes Email: ivan.ternovtsii@uzhnu.edu.ua Affiliation: https://github.com/ITernovtsii/semantic-resonance
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance but remain difficult to interpret. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models improve efficiency through sparse activation, yet typically rely on opaque, learned gating functions. While similarity-based routing (Cosine Routers) has been explored for training stabilization, its potential for inherent interpretability remains largely untapped. We introduce the Semantic Resonance Architecture (SRA), an MoE approach designed to ensure that routing decisions are inherently interpretable. SRA replaces learned gating with a Chamber of Semantic Resonance (CSR) module, which routes tokens based on cosine similarity with trainable semantic anchors. We also introduce a novel Dispersion Loss that encourages orthogonality among anchors to enforce diverse specialization. Experiments on WikiText-103 demonstrate that SRA achieves a validation perplexity of 13.41, outperforming both a dense baseline (14.13) and a Standard MoE baseline (13.53) under matched active parameter constraints (29.0M). Crucially, SRA exhibits superior expert utilization (1.0% dead experts vs. 14.8% in the Standard MoE) and develops distinct, semantically coherent specialization patterns, unlike the noisy specialization observed in standard MoEs. This work establishes semantic routing as a robust methodology for building more transparent and controllable language models.

1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized natural language processing [1, 3]. However, the opacity of these models presents substantial challenges for deployment in critical domains where decisions must be explainable and controllable [12].

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures address the computational inefficiency of dense models by conditionally activating only a subset of parameters [13]. However, standard approaches, such as the Switch Transformer [6] and GShard [10], rely on learned gating functions (typically simple linear layers) whose decision processes remain opaque.

Recent work has explored alternative routing mechanisms, including those based on cosine similarity (Cosine Routers), primarily to improve training stability and load balancing [2]. While effective for stabilization, these approaches have not focused on leveraging this mechanism to achieve inherent interpretability or enforce coherent specialization.

We propose the Semantic Resonance Architecture (SRA), an approach that leverages semantic similarity for routing, explicitly designed for interpretability. Our key innovation, the Chamber of Semantic Resonance (CSR), routes tokens to experts based on the cosine similarity between token representations and learnable semantic anchors linked to each expert. To ensure these anchors capture diverse concepts, we introduce a Dispersion Loss that actively promotes orthogonality among the anchors.

This mechanism provides notable advantages:

  1. 1.

    Inherent Interpretability: Routing decisions are directly explainable by the semantic similarity score, eliminating the opacity of learned gating.

  2. 2.

    Coherent Specialization: Aided by the Dispersion Loss, experts develop stable and semantically coherent specialization patterns, unlike the often noisy specialization observed in standard MoEs.

  3. 3.

    Improved Utilization: Semantic routing demonstrates superior synergy with training stabilization techniques, such as progressive routing, leading to better load balancing and fewer inactive experts.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce the Semantic Resonance Architecture (SRA) and a novel Dispersion Loss, demonstrating that semantic routing can be used to enforce interpretable expert specialization by design.

  • •

    We demonstrate that SRA outperforms both dense and Standard MoE baselines on WikiText-103 while maintaining the same active parameter budget and exhibiting superior expert utilization.

  • •

    We provide a comprehensive analysis showing that SRA experts develop significantly more meaningful semantic specialization than the Standard MoE baseline.

2 Related Work

2.1 Mixture of Experts and Routing Mechanisms

The MoE paradigm dates back to [9]. Recent interest has focused on scaling transformer models efficiently. Shazeer et al. [13] introduced the Sparsely-Gated MoE layer, and the Switch Transformer [6] simplified this to Top-1 routing.

These standard techniques rely on learned gating networks (e.g., linear transformations followed by softmax). While efficient, these routers offer limited insight into the rationale behind routing decisions.

Most relevant to our work is the exploration of similarity-based routing, often referred to as Cosine Routers. These have been utilized in models like XMoE [2] primarily for stabilizing training. SRA builds upon this mechanism but shifts the focus from mere stabilization to inherent interpretability. We introduce the Dispersion Loss to actively enforce semantic diversity and orthogonality, a crucial component for coherent specialization missing in prior similarity-based approaches.

2.2 Interpretability in Neural Networks

Research in interpretability includes attention visualization [16, 4], probing classifiers [15], and mechanistic interpretability [5].

For MoE architectures, post-hoc analysis of expert specialization [7] often finds that experts in standard MoEs do not specialize in recognizable semantic categories. These approaches provide interpretability after the fact rather than by design. In contrast, our semantic resonance mechanism ensures that interpretability and coherent specialization are inherent properties of the routing process itself.

3 Method

3.1 Architecture Overview

The Semantic Resonance Architecture builds upon the standard transformer decoder architecture, replacing the feed-forward network (FFN) in each layer with our Chamber of Semantic Resonance (CSR) module. The architecture utilizes standard learned embeddings with weight tying, Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) [14], and a Pre-LayerNorm configuration.

Formally, for an input sequence X∈ℝB×L×DX\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times D}, where B is the batch size, L is the sequence length, and D is the model dimension, each SRA block computes:

X′\displaystyle X^{\prime} =LayerNorm​(X)\displaystyle=\text{LayerNorm}(X) (1)
H\displaystyle H =X+MultiHeadAttention​(X′)\displaystyle=X+\text{MultiHeadAttention}(X^{\prime}) (2)
H′\displaystyle H^{\prime} =LayerNorm​(H)\displaystyle=\text{LayerNorm}(H) (3)
Y\displaystyle Y =H+CSR​(H′)\displaystyle=H+\text{CSR}(H^{\prime}) (4)

3.2 Chamber of Semantic Resonance

The CSR module routes tokens based on their "resonance" (similarity) with learnable semantic anchors.

3.2.1 Semantic Anchors and Initialization

We initialize a set of learnable semantic anchors A∈ℝN×DA\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}, where N is the number of experts. We utilize orthogonal initialization to maximize initial dispersion in the semantic space (when N≤DN\leq D):

A=orth​(randn​(N,D))A=\text{orth}(\text{randn}(N,D)) (5)

We compare this with Kaiming uniform initialization [8].

3.2.2 Resonance Calculation

For each token representation 𝐡∈ℝD\mathbf{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, we compute resonance scores with all anchors using cosine similarity. This computation is performed in FP32 for numerical stability.

ri=cos⁡(𝐡,𝐚i)=𝐡⋅𝐚i‖𝐡‖2⋅‖𝐚i‖2+ϵr_{i}=\cos(\mathbf{h},\mathbf{a}_{i})=\frac{\mathbf{h}\cdot\mathbf{a}_{i}}{\|\mathbf{h}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{a}_{i}\|_{2}+\epsilon} (6)

where 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} is the i-th semantic anchor, and ϵ=1​e−8\epsilon=1e-8.

3.2.3 Top-k Expert Selection and Execution

We select the top-k experts with the highest resonance scores. During training, Gaussian noise η∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) can optionally be added (Noisy Top-k) [13].

indices,scores\displaystyle\text{indices},\text{scores} =top_k​(𝐫+η,k)\displaystyle=\text{top\_k}(\mathbf{r}+\eta,k) (7)
weights =softmax​(scores)\displaystyle=\text{softmax}(\text{scores}) (8)

The final output is a weighted combination of the selected experts’ outputs:

𝐲=∑i∈indiceswi⋅Experti​(𝐡)\mathbf{y}=\sum_{i\in\text{indices}}w_{i}\cdot\text{Expert}_{i}(\mathbf{h}) (9)

Each expert is a two-layer feed-forward network using the GELU activation function.

3.3 Training Objectives

The total loss function combines the primary language modeling objective (ℒLM\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}) with auxiliary losses:

ℒ=ℒLM+α⋅ℒbalance+β⋅ℒdispersion+γ⋅ℒz\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}+\alpha\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{balance}}+\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{dispersion}}+\gamma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{z}} (10)

3.3.1 Load Balancing Loss

To ensure balanced utilization, we employ a load balancing loss based on the squared coefficient of variation (CV) of the routing probabilities [6].

We first calculate the average probability of selecting each expert across the batch:

Pmean=1B⋅L​∑b,lsoftmax​(𝐫b,l)P_{\text{mean}}=\frac{1}{B\cdot L}\sum_{b,l}\text{softmax}(\mathbf{r}_{b,l}) (11)

The loss is the squared CV of these mean probabilities across the N experts:

ℒbalance=N⋅Var​(Pmean)Mean​(Pmean)2+ϵ\mathcal{L}_{\text{balance}}=N\cdot\frac{\text{Var}(P_{\text{mean}})}{\text{Mean}(P_{\text{mean}})^{2}+\epsilon} (12)

3.3.2 Dispersion Loss

To encourage the semantic anchors to learn diverse and distinct concepts, we introduce a dispersion loss. This loss penalizes similarity between anchors by minimizing the average pairwise cosine similarity across all unique pairs. By pushing the anchor vectors away from each other in the semantic space, this objective encourages each expert to develop a unique specialization.

ℒdispersion=1N⁡(N−1)​∑i≠jcos⁡(𝐚i,𝐚j)\mathcal{L}_{\text{dispersion}}=\frac{1}{N(N-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\cos(\mathbf{a}_{i},\mathbf{a}_{j}) (13)

3.3.3 Router Z-Loss

For numerical stability, we explored the router z-loss [17]:

ℒz=1B⋅L​∑(log⁡(∑jexp⁡(ri​j)))2\mathcal{L}_{\text{z}}=\frac{1}{B\cdot L}\sum\left(\log\left(\sum_{j}\exp(r_{ij})\right)\right)^{2} (14)

3.4 Progressive Routing

To mitigate expert collapse often observed when training with Top-k>1 from the start, we use a progressive routing strategy. The model is trained for the initial epochs using Top-1 routing, allowing experts to establish distinct specializations. Subsequently, routing is switched to Top-2, enabling the model to leverage combinations of specialized experts.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

4.1.1 Dataset

We evaluate our approach on WikiText-103 [11]. We use byte-pair encoding (BPE) with a vocabulary size of 32,000 tokens.

4.1.2 Model Configurations

We compare SRA with a standard dense transformer and a Standard MoE model with learned gating. All models are matched for the number of active parameters per token (≈\approx29.0M). All models use D=512D=512, 4 layers, and 8 attention heads.

  • •

    SRA (Ours): Semantic routing (CSR). N=128 experts per layer (512 total). Top-k=2. Expert FFN dim (Df​fD_{ff})=1024. Total params: 558.5M. Active params: 29.0M.

  • •

    Standard MoE: Learned linear gating. N=128. Top-k=2. Df​fD_{ff}=1024. Total params: 558.5M. Active params: 29.0M.

  • •

    Dense Baseline: Standard FFN. Df​fD_{ff}=2048. Total params: 29.0M. Active params: 29.0M.

The dense baseline FFN dimension (2048) is doubled relative to the MoE expert dimension (1024) to match the active parameter count resulting from Top-2 routing.

4.1.3 Training Details

All models were trained using AdamW (β1=0.9,β2=0.95\beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.95) and the progressive routing strategy (Epochs 1-5: Top-1; Epochs 6-10: Top-2). Learning rate: 3e-4 with linear warmup (4000 steps) and cosine decay. Total batch size: 128. Sequence length: 256. Dropout: 0.1.

For SRA hyperparameters: α\alpha (balance)=0.4; β\beta (dispersion)=0.6; γ\gamma (z-loss)=0.0.

4.2 Main Results

SRA outperforms both the dense baseline and the Standard MoE model (Table 1). Crucially, SRA achieves performance parity with (slightly exceeding) the Standard MoE while providing significant advantages in interpretability.

Furthermore, SRA demonstrates vastly superior expert utilization and training stability. Despite using identical stabilization techniques, SRA resulted in only 1.0% dead experts, compared to 14.8% in the Standard MoE. This indicates that semantic routing facilitates more effective utilization of the model’s capacity.

4.3 Training Dynamics

The SRA model exhibits a distinct pattern corresponding to the progressive routing strategy (Figure 1). The shift at epoch 5 (approx 16k steps in Fig 1(b)) corresponds to the transition from Top-1 to Top-2 routing. During the Top-1 phase (0-16k steps), SRA develops initial specialization but underperforms the dense model. The transition to Top-2 (16k steps onward) immediately improves performance, allowing SRA to utilize combinations of experts and ultimately surpass the baseline. The dense baseline (Fig 1(a)) shows stable convergence to 14.13 perplexity.

4.4 Ablation Studies

We conducted ablation studies to understand the impact of routing strategies, initialization, and auxiliary losses (Table 2).

Key findings from the ablation studies:

  • •

    The Trade-off of Top-k: Increasing k improves perplexity (Top-6 PPL 11.76). However, training with Top-k>1 from the start results in substantial expert collapse (e.g., 34.4% in Top-2).

  • •

    Progressive Routing is Essential: The progressive strategy achieves an optimal balance (PPL 13.41, 1.0% dead experts).

  • •

    Impact of Initialization: Orthogonal initialization significantly outperforms Kaiming Uniform (PPL 16.95 vs 19.99 at 5 epochs), validating the hypothesis that maximizing initial dispersion is crucial for developing effective semantic specialization.

  • •

    Auxiliary Losses Matter: Both the load balancing loss and the dispersion loss are critical for performance.

5 Analysis

5.1 Expert Specialization Patterns

A primary advantage of SRA is the interpretability of its routing mechanism.

5.1.1 Semantic Resonance Architecture Specialization

Analysis of the SRA model reveals clear semantic and syntactic specialization. Table 3 presents examples from the first CSR layer.

Experts clearly learn to respond to tokens with similar properties, spanning coherent semantic categories (e.g., E42, Media) and syntactic roles (e.g., E10, Prepositions).

5.1.2 Comparison with Standard MoE

We contrast this with the Standard MoE (Learned Gating) (Table 4).

The Standard MoE leads to noisy specialization, suggesting reliance on low-level statistical features rather than coherent linguistic concepts.

5.2 Expert Utilization

Figure 2 illustrates the expert utilization patterns across all four layers of the final SRA model (trained with progressive routing). The strategy successfully mitigates expert collapse, with only 5 dead experts total.

The progressive strategy allows experts to establish specialization during the Top-1 phase (Figure 3), preventing the drastic expert collapse observed when training with Top-2 from the start (as shown in Table 2).

We also compare the utilization metrics between SRA and the Standard MoE (Table 5).

While the Standard MoE might achieve a comparable Coefficient of Variation (CV) among *active* experts, it suffers from significantly higher expert collapse (76 dead experts vs. 5 in SRA). This highlights a key advantage of SRA: grounding the routing in the geometric constraints of the semantic space inherently facilitates better overall utilization and training stability.

5.3 Semantic Anchor Dispersion

Visualization of the semantic space (e.g., t-SNE projection, see Appendix) confirms that the combination of orthogonal initialization and the dispersion loss successfully maintains separation between anchors (mean pairwise similarity: 0.073 ±\pm 0.065), preventing redundant experts.

6 Discussion

6.1 Interpretability and Coherence

The semantic resonance mechanism provides inherent interpretability by design. Routing decisions are traceable, specialization is consistent, and experts specialize in recognizable semantic categories. These properties make SRA suitable for applications where understanding the model’s internal logic is crucial.

6.2 Efficiency and Utilization

SRA maintains the same number of active parameters (29.0M) as the dense baseline, ensuring computational parity during inference. A key finding is the superior expert utilization of SRA compared to the Standard MoE (1.0% vs 14.8% dead experts), indicating enhanced training stability.

6.3 Limitations and Future Work

Our investigation highlighted areas for future research:

  1. 1.

    Scaling Behavior: Experiments were conducted at a modest scale (558.5M parameters). The behavior of SRA at billion-parameter scales remains an important area for exploration.

  2. 2.

    Quantitative Interpretability: While qualitative results are strong, future work must incorporate quantitative metrics, such as Normalized Pointwise Mutual Information (NPMI), to rigorously measure and compare specialization coherence. This is an essential next step for validating the claims of interpretability.

  3. 3.

    Controllable Output (Model Steering): Explore generated text manipulation by intervening on specific expert weights during inference (e.g., for bias reduction or style control).

6.4 Broader Impacts and Controllability

The enhanced interpretability of SRA has significant implications for model controllability. Because SRA experts specialize in coherent concepts, it becomes feasible to intervene during inference to adjust model behavior. This level of precise, semantically-grounded control is largely unavailable in dense models or standard MoEs with opaque routing.

7 Conclusion

This research introduces the Semantic Resonance Architecture (SRA), demonstrating that routing based on semantic similarity, combined with a novel Dispersion Loss, provides an effective, efficient, and interpretable alternative to learned gating functions in MoE models. Our experiments show that SRA matches the performance of Standard MoE baselines while achieving significantly higher expert utilization and exhibiting more coherent semantic specialization. The transparency offered by SRA represents a significant advancement toward developing more controllable and explainable AI systems.
